newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Some 50 bodies recovered in cyclone-hit Madagascar.
newsitem.headline: Some 50 bodies recovered in cyclone-hit Madagascar.

text.p: Rescue workers found some 50 bodies in cyclone-hit southern Madagascar and hunger faced an estimated 60,000 people sleeping in the open, state radio said on Thursday.

It said the 50 dead were recovered in destroyed homes, under fallen trees and from swollen rivers in the previous 24 hours in Vangaindrano in the southeast and rescue workers believed more would be found.
The radio had estimated some 100 people were missing since Cyclone Gretelle battered Madagascar last Friday and Saturday, the worst such storm in living memory. Vangaindrano was the worst -hit area.
Officials estimated more than 60,000 people were without shelter on the southern tip of the Indian Ocean island and even substantial buildings such as churches and hospitals had lost their roofs.
"Starvation above all threatens the victims," said the radio of the 60,000 homeless. It also spoke of the start of an epidemic of dysentery.
Travellers from the south said many people remained cut off by floodwaters.
Officials meanwhile said that interim President Norbert Ratsirahonana, who arrived in the south on Wednesday, was ready to do everything possible to ensure food and other aid arrived urgently.

The government relief effort is supported by various foreign countries and international organisations. The French military has sent a Transall transport plane carrying doctors and rescue workers and a helicopter from the island of Reunion to help.
With winds of up to 250 km (155 miles per hour), the cyclone left all 27,500 residents of Farafangana town without shelter.
The storm wreaked havoc in a rich farming zone on the world's fourth largest island producing coffee, bananas, oranges and lychees. The first planeload of aid reached the south on Sunday.
Convoys of trucks ferrying food, medicine and building materials found it hard to reach the worst-hit areas because roads were blocked in many places by floods and fallen trees.
Many villagers survived by clinging to trees to avoid being blown away. Others escaped being swept away by raging floodwaters by taking to the roofs of buildings.
Radio Madagascar has criticised the slow pace of the rescue effort. Some residents said the radio itself failed to forecast accurately the force with which the cyclone would batter the island.
Gretelle was the seventh tropical storm to hit the former French colony since the start of the cyclone season in October.
